about: Pairs of benchmark places that people often compare, most compared first. The ranking comes from one web search per pair in November 2026, counting results that name both places in their title; the first six are fixed at the top by choice. 'wines' says how the wines compare and is written only from its 'sources' (keys in SRC in src/atlas.py). How the places compare is built from the Atlas's own figures. tag: different-grapes when the places are known for different grapes, sounds-alike when they are more different than they sound.

wines.head: Pinot Noir
wines.text: Oregon Pinot Noir is often called the closest in style to Burgundy. Burgundy's own leans earthy and floral. The best red Burgundy can be kept for more than 15 years.

wines.head: Chardonnay
wines.text: Oregon Chardonnay is made around bright acidity rather than a buttery feel. Willamette growers differ on Burgundy: some say their wines are growing more like white Burgundy, while others set out not to copy it.

wines.head: Blends
wines.text: Red Bordeaux is usually a blend: Cabernet Sauvignon leads on the Left Bank and Merlot on the Right Bank. Many Napa wines also blend grapes, from the valley floor and the hillsides, and Inglenook, founded in 1879, was the first Bordeaux-style winery in the US.

wines.head: Taste and aging
wines.text: Wine Folly's side-by-side tasting suggests Bordeaux blends at about 12.5% alcohol, often surprisingly light, with earthy notes, and Napa ones at 14.5% or more, with much firmer tannins. Bordeaux's top Left Bank reds are concentrated and long-lived, and most are meant for the cellar.

wines.head: Sauvignon Blanc
wines.text: Both are high in acidity. Sancerre is mostly bone dry, made with little oak and without malolactic fermentation, and tends to be less grassy and herbaceous than New Zealand Sauvignon Blanc. Marlborough's shows vibrant fruit and very sharp acidity, with bell pepper, gooseberry and passionfruit, and a gram or two of sugar is normal there to balance the acid.

wines.head: Tempranillo
wines.text: Tempranillo leads in both. In Ribera del Duero it is called Tinto Fino, and the hot, short growing season gives a richer style, with black cherry, blackberry and dried fig. Rioja is known for vanilla from oak, with cherry, dill and cigar box.

wines.head: Aging rules
wines.text: Both use the same aging terms and rules. A red Crianza ages at least two years, one of them in oak. A Reserva ages at least three years, one in oak. A Gran Reserva ages five years before release, two of them in oak.

wines.head: Nebbiolo
wines.text: Both are Nebbiolo from the Langhe. Barbaresco gets a slight sea influence and ripens a little earlier. Its tannins are less harsh when young and soften sooner, so it does not age as long as a traditional Barolo. Barolos from La Morra and Barolo itself come closest to Barbaresco.

wines.head: Aging rules
wines.text: Barolo must age at least three years, 18 months of them in wood, and a Riserva at least five. Barbaresco must age at least two years, 9 months in wood, and a Riserva at least four.

wines.head: Made two ways
wines.text: Champagne gets its second fermentation in the bottle, from Pinot Noir, Pinot Meunier and Chardonnay, and must age at least 15 months. Most Prosecco is made from Glera and gets its second fermentation in large steel tanks, which can take as little as 30 days.

wines.head: Taste
wines.text: Prosecco is aromatic and crisp, with yellow apple, pear, white peach and apricot, and is best drunk within three to five years of its vintage. Extra Dry is its most common style.

wines.head: Made two ways
wines.text: Cava is made like Champagne, with its second fermentation in the bottle, mostly from Macabeo, Parellada and Xarel·lo, and it spends at least 9 months on its lees. Most Prosecco is made from Glera, with its second fermentation in large steel tanks, and it needs no long aging.

wines.head: Style
wines.text: Fermenting in the bottle gives Cava fine, lasting bubbles. Prosecco is fresh and fruit-driven, with apple, pear and white peach, and Extra Dry is its most common style.

wines.head: Both made in the bottle
wines.text: Both get their second fermentation in the bottle, by the traditional method. Champagne is made almost entirely from Pinot Noir, Pinot Meunier and Chardonnay. Cava is mostly Macabeo, Parellada and Xarel·lo, with Chardonnay also allowed.

wines.head: Rules
wines.text: Champagne must age at least 15 months, and vintage Champagne at least three years. Cava spends at least 9 months on its lees, and it may no longer be sold as Spanish champagne.

wines.head: Blends and single grapes
wines.text: Red Bordeaux is almost always a blend, led by Cabernet Sauvignon on the Left Bank and Merlot on the Right. Red Burgundy is Pinot Noir and white Burgundy is Chardonnay. Bordeaux ranks its producers; Burgundy ranks its vineyards.

wines.head: Taste and aging
wines.text: Left Bank reds are concentrated, tannic and long-lived. Pinot Noir is usually light to medium-bodied with lower tannin, and Burgundy's leans earthy and floral. The best grand cru Burgundy can be kept for more than 15 years.

wines.head: Sherry and Port
wines.text: Sherry is made from white grapes, mostly Palomino, and fortified after fermentation, so most Sherry is dry. Port is usually a sweet red. It is fortified partway through fermentation, which leaves sugar in the wine, and it is usually 19 to 22% alcohol.

wines.head: Aging
wines.text: Sherry ages at least two years in a solera of linked barrels and does not generally improve once bottled. Ruby Port is aged only a few years. Tawny Port ages much longer in barrel, with age statements from 10 to 50 years.

wines.head: Nebbiolo and Sangiovese
wines.text: Barolo is Nebbiolo: light in color, with strong tannin, and often said to smell of tar and roses. Brunello is 100% Sangiovese, with high acidity and flavors of blackberry, black cherry, chocolate, leather and violets.

wines.head: Aging
wines.text: Barolo must age at least three years, 18 months in wood. Brunello spends two years in oak and at least four months in bottle, and is released 50 months after the harvest. Most Brunello needs at least 10 years, and traditional Barolo can take more than 10 years to soften.

wines.head: Size and spread
wines.text: Sonoma County is far bigger than the Napa Valley AVA, about 1.14 million acres against about 253,000 acres, and it makes far more wine. Its 19 AVAs reflect how varied it is: cool-climate grapes do well in some areas and warm-climate grapes in others. Within Napa, the open southern end is cooler and the closed northern end is often much warmer.

wines.head: Grapes
wines.text: Sonoma's most planted grapes are Chardonnay, Cabernet Sauvignon and Pinot Noir, and it is also known for Merlot and Zinfandel. Napa's Chardonnay and Cabernet Sauvignon took the top places at the 1976 Paris tasting, and many Napa wines blend grapes from the valley floor and the hillsides.

wines.head: Sauvignon Blanc
wines.text: Both are Sauvignon Blanc with naturally high acidity, and only very experienced tasters can tell them apart blind. Sancerre tends to be fuller, with more pronounced aromas. Pouilly-Fumé is more perfumed and is known for a smoky bouquet.

wines.head: Soils
wines.text: Sancerre's flint soils give its most aromatic and longest-lived wines, and its clay and limestone give more body. Pouilly-Fumé grows on Kimmeridgian marl, hard limestone and flinty clay.

wines.head: Blends
wines.text: Left Bank reds are led by Cabernet Sauvignon: a top estate's blend is typically about 70% Cabernet Sauvignon, with Cabernet Franc and Merlot. Right Bank reds, around Libourne, turn that around, with about 70% Merlot.

wines.head: Style
wines.text: Left Bank reds are concentrated, tannic and long-lived, and most are meant for the cellar. Right Bank reds often have great fruit concentration and softer tannins, and they age well too. Wine Folly ties Merlot's success on the Right Bank to its clay-rich soils.

wines.head: Sangiovese
wines.text: Brunello is 100% Sangiovese. Chianti Classico is mostly Sangiovese, and white grapes have not been allowed in it since 2006.

wines.head: Style and aging
wines.text: Chianti Classico tends to be medium-bodied, with firm tannin, medium-high to high acidity and floral, cherry and light nutty notes. Brunello comes from one of the warmest, driest parts of Tuscany and has a fleshier texture, with blackberry, black cherry, chocolate, leather and violets. It spends two years in oak, is released 50 months after the harvest, and most need at least 10 years.

wines.head: Noble rot
wines.text: Both are sweet wines from grapes with noble rot. Sauternes is made from Sémillon, Sauvignon Blanc and Muscadelle. Tokaji is mainly Furmint, with Hárslevelű.

wines.head: How sweet
wines.text: For Tokaji Aszú, the rotted berries are picked one by one and trodden into a paste, and its sweetness runs from 3 to 6 puttonyos. Sauternes has no set level of sugar but must taste clearly sweet, with apricot, honey and peach and a nutty note. Both can last a very long time: Sauternes beyond 100 years, and Tokaji Eszencia 200 years or more.

wines.head: Shiraz
wines.text: Shiraz leads in both, and it is about 60% of McLaren Vale's crush. Barossa Shiraz is full-bodied, with rich chocolate and spice, and Barossa grapes can get very ripe, with high sugar and low acid, so acid is often added. McLaren Vale Shiraz shows berry and spice with some dark chocolate and liquorice, and a soft, rolling palate.

wines.head: Size and rank
wines.text: Pomerol is the smallest wine area in Bordeaux, about 800 hectares, and it has no official classification, though Pétrus and Le Pin sell at first-growth prices. Saint-Emilion covers about 5,400 hectares and has had a classification since 1955, revised about every 10 years.

wines.head: Merlot
wines.text: Merlot leads in both, often with Cabernet Franc. Wine Folly puts Pomerol's Merlot on clay-rich soils, with concentrated black cherry and plum, and Saint-Emilion's on limestone and clay, with blackcurrant and dark cherry.

wines.head: Albariño and Alvarinho
wines.text: Albariño is over 90% of the vines in Rías Baixas. In Vinho Verde, where it is called Alvarinho, it is one grape among several and most wines are blends; Vinho Alvarinho comes from Monção and Melgaço.

wines.head: Style
wines.text: Albariño has high acidity, stone fruit and a hint of salt. Most white Vinho Verde is light, about 8.5 to 11% alcohol, fresh, and released three to six months after the harvest, sometimes with a little sparkle added. Vinho Alvarinho is stronger, 11.5 to 14%, with ripe tropical aromas.

wines.head: Nebbiolo and Pinot Noir
wines.text: Barolo is made from Nebbiolo. It is medium to full-bodied, with high tannin and acidity, and is often said to smell of tar and roses. Red Burgundy is mostly Pinot Noir, which is lighter and silky, with lower tannin.

wines.head: Color and age
wines.text: Both are light in color. Barolo takes on a rust-red tinge as it matures. The best red Burgundy can be kept for more than 15 years.

wines.head: Grapes
wines.text: Paso Robles is known for Zinfandel, its heritage grape, for Cabernet Sauvignon and for Rhône-style wines, and it grew the first Syrah planted in California. Its blends often break the traditional rules. Napa's Cabernet Sauvignon and Chardonnay took the top places at the 1976 Paris tasting, and Inglenook was the first Bordeaux-style winery in the US.

wines.head: Climate
wines.text: Paso Robles is Winkler region II to III and gets 10 to 25 inches of rain a year. Napa runs from region I to III and gets 24 to 55 inches.

wines.head: Syrah and blends
wines.text: In the north, Syrah is the only red grape allowed, sometimes with a little white grape: Côte-Rôtie may add up to 20% Viognier. Southern reds are usually blends led by Grenache, with Syrah, Mourvèdre, Carignan and Cinsault, and Châteauneuf-du-Pape allows 19 varieties.

wines.head: Style
wines.text: The north is cooler, with a continental climate, and its Syrah is known for aromas of green olive and smoky bacon. The south is more Mediterranean, with hot summers. Reds from the southern Rhône's left bank are full-bodied and tannic when young, with prune, undergrowth and chocolate.
